cards.explanation: The evil is that God does not allow him to enjoy them. The man has riches, wealth and honor, and the text says God does not allow him to enjoy them. Nothing is missing from his pile except the enjoying. I think that's why the Teacher calls it a weight on mankind (Ecclesiastes 6:1).

The answer is True. The Teacher says a stranger will enjoy what the man couldn't, and then he says, "This is futile and a grievous affliction." Those are his own words for it, friends. He doesn't tiptoe around how heavy it is.

The answer is False. A hundred children and many years sound like a full life, but the Teacher says no matter how long he lives, if the man is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, a stillborn child is better off than he. So the long life and the big family don't make up for it. I think this is a hard line, and it's worth sitting with.

The answer is a stillborn child, and I think this is a heavy one, friends. The Teacher is talking about a man who is unsatisfied with his prosperity and doesn't even receive a proper burial. Next to that man, he says a stillborn child is better off. He's showing how deep the emptiness runs for a man who never enjoys what he has.

The answer is rest. The Teacher says the child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man. It's a heavy thing to say, and I think he's showing how restless a life of unenjoyed riches can be. The man has everything and can't settle into any of it.

The answer is True. After comparing the two, the Teacher asks, "Do not all go to the same place?" He asks it as a question and lets it hang there. I think he's reminding us, friends, that the length of a life doesn't change where it ends up.

The answer is that his appetite is never satisfied. The Teacher says all a man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. It's like pressing a whole batch of cookies, eating one warm, and still reaching for the next. The work goes in and the wanting is still there.

The answer is what advantage he has over the fool. The Teacher asks, "What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool?" He doesn't answer it in these verses, friends. He just lets the question sit there, and I think it's a question worth stopping to think about.

The answer is False. The text says, "Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire." What's in front of you beats the wanting that wanders off. And the Teacher still says this too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.

The answer is True. The Teacher says it's known what man is, but he cannot contend with one stronger than he. That's a plain fact about being human. I'd say it's a humbling one, friends, and I've had my share of those.

The answer is how that profits anyone. The Teacher says the more words, the more futility, and then he asks, "how does that profit anyone?" He's asking what all those words actually gain. Looks like a lot of talkers just got a little quiet.

The answer is False. The Teacher doesn't say he can tell a man what will come after him. He asks, "Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?" It's a question, not a claim, friends. Just before that, he asks who knows what is good for a man in his few days.
